topicTitle: 1.3 Relationship of Biology with Other Sciences
keyPoints: Biophysics: biological organisms follow physical principles (e.g. muscle/bone movement as levers).
Biochemistry: chemical constituents and reactions in organisms (digestion, respiration, photosynthesis).
Computational biology: data analysis and modelling of biological systems (e.g. DNA fragment mapping).
Biogeography: distribution of organisms across geographical regions.
Bio-economics: biology studied from an economic angle (e.g. crop/fish production and export value).
modelAnswer: Biology connects with several other sciences: Physics - biophysics studies how living organisms work on physical principles, e.g. the movement of muscles and bones follows lever principles. Chemistry - biochemistry studies the chemical constituents of organisms (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen etc.) and the chemical reactions inside them, such as digestion, respiration and photosynthesis. Computer - computational biology uses data analysis, mathematical modelling and computer simulation to understand biological systems, for example locating fragments of DNA on chromosomes. Geography - biogeography studies how plants and animals are distributed across different geographical regions of the world. Economics - bio-economics studies biology from an economic point of view, such as production of wheat, fish and rice and their export value.

Each link lets biology borrow instruments, mathematics and models while offering living systems as their testing ground, so the sciences advance together.

topicTitle: 1.8 Malaria an Example of Biological Method of Study
keyPoints: Recognise the problem: what causes the disease is unknown.
Make observations linking the disease to a suspected cause.
Form a testable hypothesis from the observations.
Draw an 'if...then' deduction from the hypothesis.
Test the deduction by experiment, using a control group.
Interpret results to confirm or reject the hypothesis, then report findings.
modelAnswer: The biological method helps find the cause of an infectious disease by applying its steps to a real case, as the chapter's malaria example shows. First, the problem is recognised (malaria's cause was unknown). Then observations are collected (e.g. malaria was linked to marshy areas, quinine treated it, drinking marsh water did not cause it, and Plasmodium was seen in patients' blood). From these observations a hypothesis is formed ('Plasmodium is the cause of malaria', Laveran, 1882). A deduction is drawn from the hypothesis ('if Plasmodium causes malaria, then all malaria patients should have Plasmodium in their blood'). This deduction is tested by experiment (blood of 100 patients and 100 healthy controls examined under a microscope). The results are interpreted (almost all patients had Plasmodium, only a small number of healthy controls did, and those were in the incubation period), which confirmed the hypothesis. Finally the results are reported so the finding can be used to control the disease.
stem: How may biological method help find the cause of an infectious disease?
